title: The Sky Cable paradox: From ABS-CBN’s second business to its burden
summary: Can Sky Cable become financially strong enough to stop depending on the company it was supposed to help?

blocks.text: ABS-CBN spent decades building Sky Cable into a second business that could make money outside of free television. It bought smaller cable companies, expanded into home internet and satellite TV, and borrowed billions of pesos to pay for that growth. Those choices made sense at the time, but some of the technologies Sky bet on eventually fell behind newer rivals and changing viewer habits. The bank loans, however, never went away. What started as a plan to make ABS-CBN stronger turned into another heavy financial burden for a parent company already struggling to recover from losing its free TV franchise.

Open ABS-CBN’s latest financial report and two main businesses stand out. One makes TV shows, movies, music, and live concerts. The other sells cable TV and home internet subscriptions. Both lost money in the first nine months of 2026, though they face very different problems. Content Production and Distribution—the business behind Batang Quiapo, It’s Showtime, BINI, and Star Cinema—brought in nearly P9 billion in sales, making up more than 85% of ABS-CBN’s total revenue. Still, its costs were higher than its sales, leaving it with a loss of about P2 billion. Meanwhile, the Cable TV and Broadband business—run mainly through Sky Cable Corporation and its subsidiaries—brought in only around P1.6 billion, down 41% from the same period in 2025, while its loss grew to more than P900 million. Source: ABS-CBN’s September 2026 quarterly disclosure.

Sky Cable’s problems go beyond losing subscribers and money. Between 2023 and 2025, ABS-CBN reduced the recorded the value of its Cable and Broadband business by more than P13 billion because those investments were no longer expected to earn what the company originally projected. Meanwhile, Sky Cable’s bank loans still had to be paid back, even as the business meant to pay them grew smaller.

When ABS-CBN’s Channel 2 was the Philippines’ leading free TV network, advertising paid for much of its operations. But ad money rises and falls with the economy since companies spend more when business is good and cut their ad budgets during hard times. Cable television offered something steadier: households paid monthly subscription fees, providing a more regular source of income. Sky Cable also gave ABS-CBN a way to air its own channels, including ANC, Cinema One, Myx, and Lifestyle Network, later renamed Metro.

The Lopez group grew Sky by merging it with other cable companies, including Home Cable in 2004, Destiny Cable, Solid Broadband, and UNI Cable TV in 2012, and internet provider Tri-Isys in 2017. Each acquisition expanded Sky Cable’s reach, but also meant taking on more cables, equipment, and facilities that needed to be maintained and eventually replaced. Sky Cable brought in foreign money as well. Singapore’s STT Communications invested through Sampaquita Communications under deals that later gave it 40% of Sky’s financial returns, while ABS-CBN and related Lopez companies kept the larger share. The arrangements used Philippine Depositary Receipts or PDRs, financial certificates that gave the foreign investor a right to profits linked to shares without directly owning the shares themselves. (READ: FAST FACTS: Other businesses of ABS-CBN)

Sky Cable also borrowed heavily from Philippine banks. Its financial reports list loans from BPI, Security Bank, RCBC, BDO, and other lenders over the years. In 2018 alone, Sky signed a P2-billion BDO loan to finance new equipment and fund projects, plus a separate P762 million loan to pay off an older obligation of Pilipino Cable Corporation, the operator of Home Cable. So, some loans paid for new growth, while other loans simply replaced old debts.

Back then, borrowing was a normal and reasonable way to finance a growing cable business. Laying cables and setting up equipment required huge amounts upfront, while monthly subscription payments trickled in month after month. That business model worked as long as subscribers kept paying long enough for Sky Cable to recover its investment, cover expenses, and pay off the banks. But that plan only worked if Sky Cable’s technology stayed competitive and its subscribers stayed loyal.

Much of Sky Cable’s growth depended on three big technology bets. First, it used its existing cable TV lines to deliver home internet. Instead of replacing every single wire, Sky Cable upgraded parts of the system with fiber-optic lines while keeping older copper-based coaxial cables for the final connection into many homes. Known as “hybrid” network, this was a faster and cheaper way to offer home internet than building a brand new network from scratch.

Second, SkyDirect used satellite dishes to reach households beyond Sky Cable’s wired network. That made sense in an archipelago like the Philippines where running physical cables to every town was far too expensive. This was also one of Sky Cable’s most promising growth businesses. SkyDirect had about one million subscribers in January 2019, barely three years after it was launched, according to ABS-CBN president Carlo Katigbak. By June 2020, Sky reported 1.5 million subscribers nationwide, including families in remote communities beyond the reach of regular TV signals. Satellite technology allowed Sky Cable enter those areas without laying costly cables across islands and provinces.

blocks.text: Third, Sky Cable invested in TV set-top boxes that gave subscribers more ways to watch cable channels and, later, streaming apps. By 2019, ABS-CBN’s Cable and Broadband business generated nearly P10 billion in annual revenue and reported a modest profit. The bets seemed to be paying off.
Between 2020 and 2024, four major setbacks derailed Sky Cable’s growth:

items: The June 30, 2020 NTC shutdown of SkyDirect, which ended a fast-growing satellite TV business.
The rise of online streaming, which reduced demand for traditional cable subscriptions.
The race to bring fiber internet directly into homes, which exposed the limits of Sky Cable’s older network.
The canceled P6.75-billion sale to PLDT, which left ABS-CBN with a business it had already prepared to sell.

blocks.text: The shutdown of SkyDirect. On May 5, 2020, the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) ordered ABS-CBN’s free TV and radio stations off the air after its broadcast franchise expired. On June 30, the regulator issued another order shutting SkyDirect and ABS-CBN TVplus, citing the expiration of the permits they operated under.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from ABS-CBN X posted on June 30, 2020

blocks.text: For Sky Cable, the shutdown was particularly damaging because SkyDirect was still attracting subscribers fast. From one million subscribers in January 2019, it had jumped to 1.5 million by June 2020. These were households paying monthly bills, or buying prepaid credits, to watch via satellite dishes. The service was especially useful in provincial areas where laying cable lines would have cost too much. Sky Cable had found a smart way to grow beyond the towns and cities covered by its existing wires, and that business was still booming when the government ordered it to stop. The order also required Sky Cable to refund unused prepaid credits, advance payments, and deposits.

The first two weakened Sky Cable’s TV business. The third showed the high cost of relying on an older broadband network while rivals built newer ones. The fourth deprived ABS-CBN of an opportunity to sell the company and use the proceeds for its other pressing financial needs.
The shutdown deprived Sky Cable of another major income source for ABS-CBN, and a fast-growing subscription business before its full commercial potential could be realized.

The shift to streaming. Netflix, YouTube, and other online apps offered programs that viewers could watch whenever, wherever they wanted, without paying for a traditional cable package. Sky Cable tried to fight back by launching SKY EVO in 2021, an Android-based TV box combining cable channels with streaming apps. But smart TVs, smartphones, and tablets were already letting people stream online entertainment without needing a cable subscription at all. SKY EVO was an attempt to adapt, but it could not stop the massive shift in viewing habits. (READ: Streaming services ‘winning hearts and minds’ of Filipinos, says new study)

The race for home internet. As cable TV subscribers left, Sky Cable needed broadband to become a stronger business. But rivals PLDT, Globe, and Converge ICT were pouring billions into “fiber-to-the-home” networks, which run pure fiber optic cables straight into customers houses and offices. Sky Cable’s older hybrid network could deliver fast download speeds, but traditional cable wires generally had less capacity for uploads, such as sending large files or joining video calls, and could slow down when too many neighbors went online at once.

These differences became more obvious during the pandemic, when families relied on home internet for work, online classes, video meetings, gaming, and streaming. Pure fiber networks offered much better upload speeds and room to handle heavy traffic. Sky Cable had made a technology bet that no longer fit the market. Extending the life of its older cable wires had saved money at first, but maintaining and upgrading that aging system grew more expensive just as rivals were building faster, brand new fiber networks. Sky Cable’s technology had not stopped working, but its earlier cost savings were no longer enough to keep up.

The aborted PLDT exit. In March 2023, ABS-CBN and other Sky shareholders agreed to sell the whole company to PLDT for P6.75 billion. The Philippine Competition Commission cleared the transaction in January 2024. Sky had already announced plans to discontinue cable television in February and focus strictly on broadband. Before that happened, however, both sides called off the deal because certain conditions had not been met and they could not agree on revised terms. Sky Cable kept running its cable TV service, which ABS-CBN remained responsible for a business it had already prepared to hand over.
The financial consequences from these setbacks became harder and harder to handle. Sky Cable was losing subscribers and revenue, yet its bank loans still had to be paid.

Sky Cable’s money problems appeared in two ways: It was losing money from operations, and some of the businesses and equipment it had acquired were worth less than the amounts recorded in its books. When a company buys another business, for example, it may pay extra because it expects future income from customers and a well-known brand. Accountants call this additional value goodwill. If the expected future income are no longer realistic, the company must slash that recovered value.

In 2023, ABS-CBN reduced Sky’s recorded goodwill by about P4.5 billion and lowered the value of customer accounts and other non-physical assets by nearly P1.9 billion. More cuts followed for equipment and other property. Between 2023 and 2025, the Cable and Broadband business recorded over P13 billion in these value reductions, known as impairment charges. They were accounting losses rather than cash spent during those years, but they showed that Sky Cable’s past investments would never deliver the returns ABS-CBN once expected.
The decline in the business was equally striking.
Sources: ABS-CBN annual reports and September 2026 quarterly disclosures. The massive losses in 2023 and 2024 included major cuts in asset values.
Annual revenue fell by roughly two-thirds between 2019 and 2025. Even after slashing costs, Sky Cable kept losing money.

Its debts became another major headache. By the end of 2023, Sky owed about P4.5 billion in bank loans. Because its finances were weakening, Sky Cable struggled to meet strict conditions written into those loan agreements. As a result, those loans had to be listed as short-term obligations in its financial reports, meaning the Sky Cable no longer had the automatic right to put off payments. That did not necessarily mean the banks were demanding immediate payment, but it showed how serious Sky’s borrowing problem had become.

By the end of 2025, Sky had approximately P9 billion in assets but owed around P10 billion in bank loans, unpaid bills, and other debts, meaning what it owed was roughly P1 billion more than everything it owed. ABS-CBN itself was also struggling. By September 2026, the group had nearly P12 billion in total loans and had racked up around P750 million in interest and related borrowing costs over nine months. Sky Cable was part of that debt load, while ABS-CBN’s content business was also losing money. Its auditors warned that the group’s continuing losses and money pressures created serious doubt about whether it could keep operating and paying its bills.

In July 2024, Sky Cable made a major change in its technology strategy. Instead of spending heavily to upgrade its aging cable network, it signed a deal to use Converge ICT’s fiber optic infrastructure in Metro Manila. Converge was one of the very rivals Sky Cable had been fighting for broadband customers. Under the deal, Sky Cable could use Converge’s network to offer modern fiber connections to its own subscribers, avoiding the full cost of building those connections itself. (READ: Why Converge thinks it’s the next big thing in telco)

blocks.text: The partnership gave Sky Cable a practical way to stay in the game, yet it also showed how much its strategy had changed. A company that spent decades building and upgrading its own cable network was now relying on a competitor’s infrastructure to give customers what they wanted.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from Sky Cable Corp. statement on July 22, 2024.

blocks.text: Sky also needed breathing room from its banks. In February 2025, BDO, BPI, RCBC, and Security Bank agreed to change the repayment terms of P4.25 billion in loans, pushing some deadlines as far as 2032. The deal gave Sky Cable more time to pay and eased some of the financial conditions it had to meet. But the loans were not forgiven.

The debt deal produced an unusual result in Sky Cable’s 2025 financial report: an accounting gain of about P1.4 billion, even though no actual cash entered Sky Cable’s bank account. That gain came from how accountants recalculated the value of the loans after their terms changed. It helped shrink Sky’s reported loss for 2025, but the business still had to pay back every peso under the new schedule.

The financial troubles of Sky Cable came up again when ABS-CBN brought in new investors in 2026. In August, the media company announced a P6 billion investment deal: P3.5 billion from I&C Holdings, P2.2 billion from three Lopez family investment companies, and P300 million from Lopez Inc. The fresh cash is meant to support operations, pay overdue bills, and cut down bank debt.

blocks.caption: After Gabby sold to Ramon Ang, Piki Lopez is securing the family’s crown jewels

blocks.text: But I&C, the largest new investor, wanted protection from some of ABS-CBN’s existing money troubles. Under the agreement, ABS-CBN promised to pay for any Sky Cable worker separation costs above ₱402 million, along with certain other Sky-related bills. I&C also required that any updates to ABS-CBN’s loans with BPI and UnionBank leave the network with terms at least as good as before. Simply put, the new investor wanted a guarantee that renegotiating those bank loans wouldn’t leave ABS-CBN in a worse financial spot.

On top of that, I&C demanded protection from other identified losses worth over P3 billion. The message was unmistakable: I&C was ready to invest, but only with strict guardrails against ABS-CBN’s existing risks. Even so, those guardrails didn’t erase Sky’s debts, and they didn’t mean ABS-CBN was planning to sell or close Sky down.

That detail matters. I&C was not refusing to touch any risk connected to Sky Cable, and the P402-million threshold was not a cap on everything ABS-CBN might still have to spend on the subsidiary. Rather, the investor wanted legal protection from specific liabilities. In business, this is known as ring-fencing: drawing clear boundaries around certain financial risks so they do not automatically become an unlimited obligation for the new investor.

For ABS-CBN, this meant Sky’s financial problems were no longer just a matter of managing a troubled subsidiary. They had become a key bargaining chip in bringing fresh money into the parent company. The investment deal did not establish that Sky would be sold, closed, or separated from ABS-CBN, but it showed that Sky’s lingering debts were serious enough for a new investor to demand protection.

Sky Cable’s story shows how a company can borrow and invest in technologies that make total commercial and financial sense at the time, only to find out later that the market has moved in another direction. Its hybrid cable network fell behind newer fiber internet, its satellite TV business was shut down by regulators, and its attempt to modernize cable TV could not stop the shift to streaming. Those technology bets lost much of their expected value, yet the debts they created remained.

Sky Cable is now trying to survive by renting space on a rival’s network and taking more time to pay its banks. Neither move guarantees that lost customers will come back or that the business will make a profit again.

Sky Cable once gave ABS-CBN a way to earn steady money outside of free TV. Almost four decades later, the question has reversed: Can Sky Cable become financially strong enough to stop depending on the company it was supposed to help? – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.
